claims.text: Plastic deformation in quaternary equiatomic FCC alloys under uniaxial tension is primarily governed by dislocation glide.
Stacking-fault formation is a primary deformation process in these alloys.
FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC transformations occur only at high strain rates or low temperatures.
High strain rates or low temperatures suppress stacking-fault energy.
A stacking-fault energy above 30 mJ/m² prevents deformation-induced phase transformations.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate when stacking-fault energy exceeds 30 mJ/m².
Equiatomic CoCrFeNi and AlCrFeNi variants can provide a single-phase FCC initial state.
The relevant single-phase FCC alloys have grain sizes of 10–100 μm.
The initial alloy has a stacking-fault energy above 25 mJ/m².
Dislocation networks and stacking faults are the principal structural mediators of deformation.
HCP or BCC martensite can form during severe deformation.
At moderate or high stacking-fault energy, deformation is dominated by dislocation glide and cross-slip.
Dislocation pile-ups produce strain hardening in the proposed alloy class.
At cryogenic temperature or low stacking-fault energy, deformation-induced phase transformations and twinning become active.
Deformation twinning enhances strain hardening under cryogenic conditions.
Yield strength increases as temperature decreases and strain rate increases.
Dislocation density dominates microstructural evolution at moderate strains.
Phase transformations emerge only at high strains or low temperatures.
Pure Ni and Cu exhibit dislocation-dominated plasticity with minimal phase transformation under comparable conditions.
If no phase transformation occurs at 77 K and 10³ s⁻¹ while yield strength remains strain-rate-insensitive, dislocation glide alone cannot explain the behavior and the hypothesis is falsified.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that suppression of phase transformations leaves dislocation-based plasticity and produces diminished strain-rate sensitivity, but the proposed falsification criterion treats the same combination—no transformation and strain-rate-insensitive yield—as evidence that dislocation glide cannot explain the behavior.

The hypothesis restricts transformations to high strain rates or low temperatures, whereas the predicted outcome substitutes high strain for high strain rate. These are distinct boundary conditions and can yield incompatible predictions at high strain under a moderate rate.
